name: Quechua
variety: Cusco-Collao Quechua as spoken in and around Cusco, Peru. eSpeak NG accepts the letters for aspirated and ejective stops (ph th chh kh qh, p' t' ch' k' q'), which exist only in the Cusco-Collao and Bolivian varieties, not in Ayacucho-Chanka; its number words and pronouns (pichqa, ñuqa, qam, ñuqanchik) use the unified Southern Quechua spelling that Ayacucho shares. Acoustic figures come from the closely related Cochabamba (Bolivian) variety
sources: Cusihuamán G., Antonio (1976). Gramática quechua: Cuzco-Collao. Lima: Ministerio de Educación and Instituto de Estudios Peruanos.
Cerrón-Palomino, Rodolfo (1987). Lingüística quechua. Cusco: Centro de Estudios Rurales Andinos Bartolomé de las Casas.
Mannheim, Bruce (1991). The Language of the Inka since the European Invasion. Austin: University of Texas Press.
Adelaar, Willem F. H. with Muysken, Pieter C. (2004). The Languages of the Andes. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press.
Parker, Steve & Weber, David (1996). Glottalized and aspirated stops in Cuzco Quechua. International Journal of American Linguistics 62.
Gallagher, Gillian (2016). Vowel height allophony and dorsal place contrasts in Cochabamba Quechua. Phonetica 73(2), 101-119.
Gallagher, Gillian & Whang, James (2014). An acoustic study of trans-vocalic ejective pairs in Cochabamba Quechua. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 44(2), 133-154.
Gallagher, Gillian (2011). Acoustic and articulatory features in phonology: the case for [long VOT]. The Linguistic Review 28.
O'Rourke, Erin (2009). Phonetics and phonology of Cuzco Quechua declarative intonation: an instrumental analysis. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 39(3), 291-312.
O'Rourke, Erin (2007). Intonation in Quechua: questions and analysis. Paper for the workshop on intonational phonology at the 16th International Congress of Phonetic Sciences, Saarbrücken.
contrasts: three-way laryngeal contrast in stops and affricates at five places: plain, aspirated, ejective (tanta 'gathering', thanta 'worn out', t'anta 'bread')
velar versus uvular stops: k kʰ kʼ versus q qʰ qʼ
three native vowel phonemes /i a u/; [e] and [o] are their allophones next to uvulars and are phonemes only in Spanish loans, which is why they are listed last among the vowels
palatal ɲ and ʎ versus alveolar n and l
no voiced stops in native words
allophony: /i u/ are lowered to [e o] or [ɛ ɔ] when a uvular precedes or follows, also across an intervening coda consonant (sunqu with [o], urqu with [o]) and across a morpheme boundary; the lowered vowel is itself a cue to the uvular
/a/ is backed to [ɑ] next to a uvular
in Cusco, stops at the end of a syllable are fricatives: /p/ is [ɸ], /t/ is [s], /tʃ/ is [ʃ], /k/ is [x], /q/ is [χ] (llaqta with [χ], pichqa pronounced pisqa)
in Bolivian varieties plain /q/ is commonly a voiced uvular continuant [ʁ] (Gallagher 2016)
ejectives have a long voice onset time and a strong burst; creak on the following vowel is rare (Gallagher & Whang 2014)
aspirates and ejectives occur only in roots, only in syllable onsets and at most once per root, on the first stop of the root
roots that begin with a vowel are pronounced with an initial glottal stop
/n/ is velar [ŋ] at the end of a word and takes the place of a following stop
syllable_structure: CV(C); an onset is always present phonetically, no clusters inside a syllable
phonotactics: codas in roots are fricatives, nasals, liquids or glides; aspirates and ejectives are excluded from codas and from suffixes
two ejectives or two aspirates do not occur in one root; an ejective or aspirate in the second syllable requires the first consonant not to be a stop
glides after vowels (ay, aw, uy) are codas, not diphthongs

stress.rule: Stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the word and moves rightwards as suffixes are added; final stress occurs with emphatic suffixes and in a few exclamations (arí 'yes') and is written with an acute accent.
stress.cues: a pitch peak inside the stressed syllable (all nuclear and 86 percent of prenuclear peaks in O'Rourke 2007); secondary stress on the first syllable is weak

rhythm.vowel_reduction: none reported as a phonological rule
rhythm.notes: The rhythm class and the degree of final lengthening are not established by measurement in the sources consulted; both values are defaults for a language with simple CV(C) syllables and no vowel reduction. In Cochabamba nonce roots of the shape CVCV the first vowel averaged 129 ms (an earlier experiment reported in Gallagher & Whang 2014).

length.notes: No length contrasts in Cusco Quechua.

voice_onset_time_ms.source: Gallagher & Whang 2014, Cochabamba Quechua, eight speakers, ejectives pooled over places: model estimate 91 ms word-medially, about 11 ms more word-initially; plain and aspirated values (Gallagher 2011) not reproduced here

intonation.declarative: a pitch accent (H* or L+H*) on the stressed syllable of nouns, verbs and other content words; each later peak is usually lower than the one before (downstep in 63 percent of peak pairs); low final boundary (L%)
intonation.yes_no_question: marked by the suffix -chu and ending low (L%), like statements; echo, confirmation and resumptive questions without -chu end in a rise (H%) or a high fall (HL%) with expanded range
intonation.wh_question: question word with an accent; ends low (L%)
intonation.continuation: intermediate phrases end in L- or, less often, H-
intonation.accent_shape: L+H* with the low at the start of the stressed syllable and the peak inside it; the peak is not delayed to the following syllable
intonation.notes: After O'Rourke (2007, 2009): ten male speakers from Cusco, semi-spontaneous speech, peaks of roughly 105 to 140 Hz in the examples shown.

problems: no vowel lowering next to uvulars: qilla, sunqu, urqu keep [i] and [u]; [e o] appear only if the text is written with e and o
ch' fails at the start of a word: ch'aki is spelled out letter by letter, while sach'a inside a word works
every ejective is followed by a separate glottal stop; p' and ch' use the recordings of aspirated stops and q' uses a fricative noise, so only k' and t' have an ejective burst
aspirated stops are a plain stop followed by a separate [h], with no single aspirated phonemes
stops at the end of a syllable stay stops; the Cusco fricatives [ɸ s ʃ x χ] are missing
final stress written with an acute accent is ignored (arí is stressed on the first syllable)
the number words are transcribed with velar k for uvular q (pusak, iskun, sukta, waranka), and numbers above nine are read digit by digit
good: a uvular stop q distinct from velar k
ll as [ʎ], ñ as [ɲ], r as a tap

notes: The three-vowel and five-vowel spellings are both in use for Cusco Quechua; the five-vowel spelling writes the lowered allophones as e and o.
